### Observed differences

- The resources executing seven activities — A01, A03, A10, A13, A14, A17 and A22 — changed markedly. In the earlier window, each activity was handled mainly by a stable set of about ten frequently used resources with individual shares of roughly 4–11 in 100; in the later window, most of these lost nearly all their share and a largely different set, previously outside the top ranks, took over. On A01, for example, eight resources that together held about 40 in 100 assignments fell to about zero, while newcomers such as User_41 (about 6 in 100) and User_39 (up from about 4 to about 9 in 100) replaced them. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]
- The same two groups recur across activities: User_46 was the most frequent resource on six of the seven activities in the earlier window (about 7–11 in 100 each) and afterwards dropped out of the top ranks everywhere except A22, where it fell to about 5 in 100; User_39 gained share on all seven activities, reaching about 8–13 in 100 (about 13 in 100 on A22, up from about 7). [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]
- A10 additionally became far less concentrated: in the earlier window its seven most used resources covered about 86 in 100 executions (largest about 17 in 100); in the later window they retained only about 37 in 100, and executions by resources outside the ten most frequent rose from about 14 to about 52 in 100. [ASSIGN003]
- For the A09–A04 activity pair, the elapsed time between consecutive completion events was redistributed rather than uniformly shifted: the median interval rose only from about 1.0 to about 1.2 minutes and the upper quartile from about 1.3 to about 1.4 minutes, but the mean nearly doubled (about 1.0 to about 1.9 minutes) because the spread grew more than twenty-fold (from about 0.3 to about 7 minutes), i.e. a minority of much longer intervals appeared; the number of observed intervals fell from 132 to 105. [TWAIT001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a change in resource allocation as a possibility: the execution of activities A01, A03, A10, A13, A14, A17 and A22 moved from one group of resources to a largely different group, with A10 additionally spreading from a few heavily used resources to many occasionally used ones. The resource family produced 7 qualifying items where about 0.007 would be expected if nothing had changed — far beyond what chance produces — and all seven point the same way, with a common set of earlier resources losing share and a common set of replacements gaining it; each profile rests on roughly 130–270 executions per window, and each difference exceeds all but about 1 of 2,000 random re-splits. The control-flow family produced no items (0 of 34 tested units against about 0.17 expected), so the difference is confined to allocation and is not accompanied by structural change at these thresholds. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

Limitations: the seven profiles probably describe one shared reallocation rather than independent changes, and the data show only who executed the activities — a different mix of cases reaching these activities in the later window could produce new resource profiles without any reallocation of the same work, and the evidence cannot rule this out. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

Other differences: the A09–A04 timing redistribution described above stands alone (1 item against about 0.015 expected in its family, i.e. within what an unchanged process typically produces) and does not by itself support a change in timing. [TWAIT001]
